questions.questionText: Reiaan uses a grid with pins and threads to represent his room. If he represents the room using a scale of $1 \text{ cm} : 1 \text{ foot}$, and the room floor is $12 \text{ ft} \times 10 \text{ ft}$, what are the dimensions of the grid on the map?
questions.explanationAnswer: Given the scale $1 \text{ cm} = 1 \text{ foot}$, a room of $12 \text{ ft} \times 10 \text{ ft}$ maps directly to $12 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$.
questions.explanationQuestion: The question tests the application of scale conversion in a geometric grid layout.

questions.questionText: Refer to Fig 1.1. If Reiaan wants to place a new item at coordinates $(5, 5)$ on his grid, explain why the position of windows cannot be marked on this floor map.

subjective_evaluation_points.point: Explains that the map is a 2D representation of the floor surface only.
States that windows are typically located on vertical walls, which have a height dimension not captured by a floor-only coordinate system.

questions.explanationAnswer: The map provides a top-down view (floor plan). Windows are on the walls (vertical plane). Since the coordinates $(x, y)$ only describe the floor surface, the vertical placement of windows cannot be represented.
questions.explanationQuestion: This tests the understanding of limitations of 2D floor mapping.
questions.correctAnswer: The map is a 2D floor plan and does not account for the vertical height of walls where windows are placed.

questions.questionText: Assertion: Brahmagupta's formalization of negative numbers was essential for the development of the four-quadrant Cartesian plane. Reason: Without negative coordinates, we cannot represent points to the left of the y-axis or below the x-axis.
questions.explanationAnswer: Brahmagupta's work on zero and negative integers provided the algebraic basis for extending the number line into a plane where directions are represented by signs.
questions.explanationQuestion: Evaluates the historical significance of negative numbers in coordinate geometry.

questions.questionText: Assertion: The point $(3, 5)$ is the same as $(5, 3)$ in a Cartesian coordinate system. Reason: The coordinates are interchangeable because addition is commutative.
questions.explanationAnswer: In a Cartesian system, order matters. $(x, y)$ defines a unique distance from the axes. $(3, 5) \neq (5, 3)$.
questions.explanationQuestion: Tests the understanding of ordered pairs in coordinate geometry.

questions.questionText: In the context of Reiaan's room (Fig 1.3), which of the following statements correctly describe the placement of objects?

options.optionText: The origin $(0,0)$ is at the corner of the room.
Points on the y-axis represent the left wall of the room.
The wardrobe width is measured along the y-axis.
The bed position spans multiple x and y values.

multi: The origin $(0,0)$ is at the corner of the room.
Points on the y-axis represent the left wall of the room.
The bed position spans multiple x and y values.
questions.explanationAnswer: Based on Fig 1.3, the origin is a corner, the y-axis aligns with the left wall, and the bed is an area object. The wardrobe width is aligned with the x-axis, not the y-axis.
questions.explanationQuestion: Tests the ability to interpret a physical layout mapped to a coordinate grid.

questions.questionText: In a city grid where streets are $200 \text{ m}$ apart, if the intersection of the $2^{nd}$ street (North-South) and $5^{th}$ street (East-West) is denoted as $(2, 5)$, then the intersection of the $4^{th}$ N-S street and $3^{rd}$ E-W street is denoted as ______.
questions.explanationAnswer: The convention provided is (N-S street, E-W street). Thus, 4th N-S and 3rd E-W corresponds to $(4, 3)$.
questions.explanationQuestion: Tests the application of coordinate conventions to real-world grid systems.
